title: Jude and the Alibi
premise: Retired detective Xanthe Eriksen has spent fifteen years hiding behind the counter of a failing coastal bookshop, until a confession letter arrives postmarked one day after the funeral of Danny Voss—the boy who vanished thirty years ago, the case that ended Xanthe's career. The letter names three people, each with an airtight alibi Xanthe themselves helped build decades ago. As Xanthe reopens old wounds among the town's founding families, they discover the alibis were woven together deliberately, and that someone in town has been killing to keep them intact. In the end, Xanthe must choose between exposing the truth and protecting the found family of misfits who've become their only home—resolving it when the winter tide finally gives up what it took: Danny's remains, and evidence that convicts the one person Xanthe loves most.
about_author: Lena Joubert is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper reporter who covered cold cases along the Atlantic seaboard for two decades. They write mysteries about towns that keep their secrets the way the sea keeps its dead.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Three days after Danny Voss's funeral—a funeral for a boy missing thirty years—a confession letter arrives at Eriksen Books, postmarked the day after the service. Xanthe reads it twice, burns no copy, tells no one. The emotional beat is dread wrapped in professional habit: the letter is addressed to 'The detective who owes me.'

chapters.title: The Inventory of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. We meet the bookshop's ragtag orbit: Marisol the runaway clerk, Gus the retired ferryman, and Odile, the coroner who looks the other way on late fees. Xanthe catalogs the letter's claims against memory. Beat: reluctant recognition that the confession knows details never made public—including that Xanthe falsified one alibi.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Low Tide
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, with flashback threads to 1994. The original case: Danny Voss vanished during the Founders' Regatta; three suspects had alibis Xanthe helped verify as a young officer. The case broke Xanthe's career when evidence went missing. Beat: guilt resurfacing like something buoyant finally loosed from the bottom.

chapters.title: Three Names, One Letter
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The letter names Bram Voss (Danny's brother), Councilwoman Hettie Marsh, and Father Anselm Cole. All three attended the funeral; all three are still in town. Xanthe begins quiet surveillance. Beat: the hunter's cold pleasure returning, unwelcome as an old injury aching before rain.

chapters.title: What Marisol Saw
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The clerk noticed a stranger buying tide tables and nautical charts the week before the funeral—and again after. She covers for Xanthe's distraction but starts her own notebook. Beat: loyalty forming into purpose; Marisol decides the bookshop's broken family is worth investigating for.

chapters.title: Bram Voss Drinks Alone
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe approaches Bram under the pretext of appraising his mother's book collection. Bram is grief-hollowed and strangely relieved someone is asking. He reveals Danny wrote him a letter years ago that he never opened. Beat: pity complicating suspicion—Bram's alibi was the strongest, and the saddest.

chapters.title: The Unopened Letter
chapters.summary: Alternating Xanthe/Marisol POV. Danny's letter to Bram, finally read, says only: 'If I go out, it wasn't the water that decided.' Meanwhile Hettie Marsh makes a generous donation offer to keep the bookshop afloat—an obvious bribe or genuine kindness? Beat: the trap of gratitude.

chapters.title: Alibi, Woven
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Reconstructing the night of the regatta, Xanthe realizes the three alibis corroborate each other in a perfect closed loop—too perfect. Someone designed them together. And the officer who verified them all was Xanthe's old partner, Ray Delacroix, now dying in a care home. Beat: vertigo—the case was rigged from inside.

chapters.title: Ray Delacroix, Mostly Gone
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Ray, deep in dementia, surfaces long enough to say: 'You signed it, Xan. You signed all three.' Then he weeps and calls Xanthe by his dead wife's name. Beat: horror that Xanthe's own hands wove part of the web—memory itself becomes unreliable testimony.

chapters.title: Fire at the Chart Room
chapters.summary: Gus's POV. A fire guts the harbor chart room where regatta records were archived. Gus pulls the night watchman out and glimpses a figure in a bookshop tote bag—Marisol's. Beat: fear curdling toward betrayal; the family Xanthe built may contain the arsonist, or be targeted by one.

chapters.title: Odile's Second Drawer
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The coroner reveals Danny's original file contained a preliminary autopsy request that was quashed—signed off by Hettie Marsh's father, then-sheriff. Odile has kept a duplicate for thirty years out of stubbornness. Beat: quiet courage; the institutional record was always a crime scene.

chapters.title: Hettie Marsh Offers Everything
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Hettie corners Xanthe: full funding for the shop, a seat on the library board, anything—if Xanthe stops asking questions before the anniversary gala. Her alibi that night: hosting the regatta dinner, witnessed by forty people. Beat: temptation sharpened by certainty that innocence wouldn't need to buy silence this hard.

chapters.title: Father Cole Confesses Something Else
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Anselm admits he heard a deathbed-adjacent confession thirty years ago—but seal-bound, he can't name the penitent. He can say only that the sin confessed was not killing Danny, but burying something for someone. Beat: moral anguish; the priest's integrity versus justice outside the law.

chapters.title: The Tote Bag
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Confronting Marisol about the fire, Xanthe finds her notebook instead: she'd been tracking the stranger buying charts—it was Bram Voss wearing a stolen shop bag. Relief, then worse: Marisol followed Bram to the old lifeboat station and saw him digging. Beat: the found family holds; the suspect list narrows and darkens.

chapters.title: What the Lifeboat Station Kept
chapters.summary: Xanthe and Marisol's POV, alternating. At the station they find fresh excavation—and older traces: a child's shoe, corroded chain. Bram arrives, desperate, admitting he's been searching for Danny's body for years because Danny's letter implied he knew he was in danger from someone 'at the head table.' Beat: grief aligning former adversaries.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Gala
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. At the Founders' Gala, Xanthe publicly announces the case is reopened, forcing every alibi-holder into one room. Hettie's composure cracks; Anselm leaves mid-speech; someone slips a note into Xanthe's pocket: 'Stop, or the shop burns next.' Beat: open declaration of war.

chapters.title: Arson, Attempted
chapters.summary: Gus and Marisol's POV. The bookshop is set alight at 3 a.m.; Gus, sleeping in the back room since the chart fire, raises the alarm. The shop survives barely; a matchbook from the regatta yacht club is found in the alley. Beat: rage crystallizing into resolve—they came for the family, and the family stands.

chapters.title: The Tide Gives Up What It Took
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A winter storm surge erodes the dunes near the lifeboat station, exposing remains and a rotted satchel: Danny's effects, including a second letter naming his killer—not as accusation but as plea. The evidence points to Ray Delacroix's cover-up protecting someone still alive. Beat: the sea testifies at last.

chapters.title: Signed, Xanthe
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Reconstructing Ray's words, Xanthe confronts the unbearable possibility: young Xanthe signed the alibi verifications without checking, eager to close the case, and the real killer has known for thirty years that Xanthe is the loose thread. The confession letter wasn't from the killer—it was bait to draw Xanthe back. Beat: self-indictment; the detective becomes the flaw in the design.

chapters.title: The Penitent at the Door
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, climax part one. The killer comes to the shop at closing: Hettie Marsh, whose father killed Danny accidentally during a confrontation and forced Ray and young Xanthe's paperwork to bury it. Hettie has killed since—the watchman, the fires—to protect the family name. She offers Xanthe the same choice her father offered Ray. Beat: the choice between truth and survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Climax part two, multiple POVs. Xanthe records Hettie's confession via the shop's ancient answering machine while Gus and Marisol stall her; Odile arrives with the suppressed autopsy duplicate. Cornered, Hettie confesses fully—her father's act, her own murders—before state police, tipped by Anselm breaking his seal through a technicality, take her. Beat: catharsis; the law arrives only because the family held the line first.

chapters.title: Eriksen Books, Open Sign Lit
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, resolution. Danny is buried properly beside his mother; Bram and Xanthe lay the unopened-letter guilt down together. Ray dies peacefully, forgiven if not absolved. The shop reopens with a new shelf: books on tides, donated by the town. Xanthe keeps the confession letter framed behind the register—as a reminder that staying invisible was never really an option. Beat: earned peace; found family, chosen truth.
